title: Unique 3-Digit Even Numbers
statement:
Every entry of `digits` is a single digit from 0 to 9. A three-digit number is built by choosing three different positions of `digits` and placing their digits, in any order, as the hundreds, tens and units digit. So a digit value can appear in a number at most as many times as it occurs in `digits`.

A built number counts only if it is even and its hundreds digit is not 0. Return how many different numbers can be built; a number that can be built in several ways is counted once.
notes:
## Intuition

There are at most 10 digits, so there are at most 10 · 9 · 8 = 720 ordered ways to pick the positions of the hundreds, tens and units digits. Trying all of them is cheap. The one catch is that equal digits at different positions build the same number more than once, so the numbers go into a set and the answer is its size. (Checking each of the 450 even numbers from 100 to 998 against the digit counts works too.)

## Approach

1. For each position `i` of the hundreds digit, skip it when `digits[i]` is 0, since a number cannot start with 0.
2. For each other position `j`, use `digits[j]` as the tens digit.
3. For each position `k` different from `i` and `j` whose digit is even, add `digits[i] * 100 + digits[j] * 10 + digits[k]` to `seen`.
4. Return `seen.size`.

## Example 1, step by step

`digits = [1, 2, 3, 4]`. The units digit must be 2 or 4.

- Hundreds digit 1: 124, 132, 134 and 142.
- Hundreds digit 2: only 4 can end it, giving 214 and 234.
- Hundreds digit 3: 312, 314, 324 and 342.
- Hundreds digit 4: only 2 can end it, giving 412 and 432.

No number repeats here, so `seen` ends with 12 numbers. 222 is impossible because only one position holds a 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³), which is at most 720 triples for n ≤ 10.
- Space: O(1): the set never holds more than the 450 even three-digit numbers.

## Pitfalls

- Count different numbers, not different picks: `[6, 6, 6]` has 6 ordered picks but builds only 666.
- Choosing positions, not values, makes each copy of a digit usable once, so `[1, 2, 3, 4]` cannot build 222.
- Only the hundreds digit must be nonzero; 0 is fine in the tens or units place, as in 202 and 220 for `[0, 2, 2]`.
- Evenness depends on the units digit alone, which must be 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | the different numbers built so far |
| `n` | number of digits |
| `i`, `j`, `k` | positions used for the hundreds, tens and units digit |

narration.2: The set keeps each built number once, however many ways it can be built.
narration.4: Try every position for the hundreds digit.
narration.5: A number cannot start with 0, so a zero cannot be the hundreds digit.
narration.6: Try every position for the tens digit...
narration.7: ...except the one already holding the hundreds digit.
narration.8: Try every position for the units digit.
narration.9: It must differ from both positions in use, so each copy of a digit is used at most once.
narration.10: An odd units digit makes the number odd, so skip it.
narration.11: Build the number and add it to the set; a repeat changes nothing.
narration.15: The set's size is the number of different even numbers.
